topics.title: Overview of Companies Act, 2013 & Section 1
explain: The Companies Act, 2013 consolidated and updated Indian corporate law to support modern economic growth.
It received Presidential assent on 29th August 2013 and was published in the Gazette on 30th August 2013.
The Act comprises 470 sections, 7 schedules, and 29 chapters.
Section 1 extends to the whole of India and came into force immediately on 30th August 2013.
It applies to companies under this Act or previous law, insurance, banking, electricity companies, and special Act bodies.
If the Companies Act conflicts with sector-specific laws like the Banking Regulation Act or Insurance Act, the sector law prevails.

flow.title: Applicability Check under Section 1
steps: Apply Companies Act for general provisions

topics.example: ABC Ltd. was incorporated in 1972 under the Companies Act, 1956. The Companies Act, 2013 automatically applies to it.
remember: Sector-specific laws override Companies Act in case of conflict
mistakes: Assuming the Companies Act overrides the Banking Regulation Act or Electricity Act during a legal conflict.

quiz.q: When did the Companies Act, 2013 receive the assent of the President of India?
quiz.why: The Act received Presidential assent on 29th August 2013 and was notified in the Official Gazette on 30th August 2013.

quiz.q: If a provision of the Companies Act, 2013 conflicts with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which law applies to a banking company?
quiz.why: Specific sector laws override Companies Act provisions to the extent of any inconsistency.

topics.title: Types of Companies & Special Classifications
explain: Company [Sec 2(20)] is an entity incorporated under this Act or any previous company law.
Private Company [Sec 2(68)] restricts share transfers, caps members at 200, and prohibits public security subscriptions.
Public Company [Sec 2(71)] is not a private company; a private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public.
One Person Company (OPC) [Sec 2(62)] is a private company with only one individual as its member.
Small Company [Sec 2(85)] is a non-public private company with paid-up capital <= 10 Crore AND turnover <= 100 Crore.
Holding/subsidiary companies, Section 8 companies, and special Act companies can never be classified as small companies.
Government Company [Sec 2(45)] has at least 51% paid-up capital (or total voting power) held by Central or State Governments.

flow.title: Testing Small Company Eligibility
steps: Check if entity is private company
Verify paid-up capital up to 10 Crore

topics.example: H Ltd holds 100% shares of S Pvt Ltd. Even if S Pvt Ltd has capital of 1 Crore and turnover of 5 Crore, it cannot be a small company because it is a subsidiary of H Ltd.
remember: Small Company thresholds: Paid-up capital <= 10 Crore & Turnover <= 100 Crore
Government Company threshold: At least 51% shareholding or total voting power by Government
Private subsidiary of a public company is deemed a public company
mistakes: Thinking a Section 8 company or a public company can claim Small Company status.

quiz.q: What is the maximum prescribed limit of paid-up share capital for a company to qualify as a Small Company under Section 2(85)?
quiz.why: Under the prescribed rules for Section 2(85), paid-up capital must not exceed 10 Crore rupees.

quiz.q: Which of the following entities can NEVER be classified as a Small Company under Section 2(85)?
quiz.why: Section 2(85) explicitly excludes Section 8 companies, holding/subsidiary companies, and special Act entities from being small companies.

topics.title: Holding, Subsidiary, Associate Companies & Control
explain: Holding Company [Sec 2(46)] is a company of which one or more other companies are subsidiary companies.
Subsidiary Company [Sec 2(87)] is an entity where the holding company controls Board composition OR exercises > 50% voting power.
Control over Board composition exists if a company can appoint or remove all or a majority of directors.
Associate Company [Sec 2(6)] is one where another company has significant influence (at least 20% total voting power or business control).
Associate company status includes joint venture arrangements but excludes subsidiary companies.
Shares held in a fiduciary capacity (such as a trustee) are excluded when determining associate or subsidiary relationships.

flow.title: Determining Inter-Corporate Relationship
steps: Identify shareholding or voting power held
Exclude shares held in fiduciary capacity
If voting power 20% to 50%: Associate Company
If majority Board appointed: Subsidiary Company

topics.example: ABC Ltd holds 25% of the total voting power in XYZ Ltd. XYZ Ltd is an Associate Company of ABC Ltd, provided it is not its subsidiary.
remember: Significant Influence = Control of at least 20% total voting power
Subsidiary Status = Controls Board composition OR > 50% total voting power
mistakes: Including shares held in a fiduciary capacity when calculating holding-subsidiary or associate company status.

quiz.q: What minimum percentage of total voting power creates 'Significant Influence' for an Associate Company under Section 2(6)?
quiz.why: Significant influence means control of at least 20% of total voting power or control of business decisions under an agreement.

quiz.q: If Company A controls the composition of the Board of Directors of Company B, Company B is classified as a:
quiz.why: Controlling the composition of the Board of Directors establishes a subsidiary relationship under Section 2(87).

topics.title: Share Capital, Free Reserves & Net Worth
explain: Authorised/Nominal Capital [Sec 2(8)] is the maximum share capital authorised by a company's memorandum.
Issued Capital [Sec 2(50)] is the portion of capital offered by the company from time to time for subscription.
Paid-up Share Capital [Sec 2(64)] is the total money credited as paid up equivalent to amounts received for shares.
Free Reserves [Sec 2(43)] are reserves available for dividend distribution, excluding unrealised/notional gains and asset revaluations.
Net Worth [Sec 2(57)] equals paid-up capital + profit reserves + securities premium + P&L credit MINUS losses and deferred expenditure.
Net Worth explicitly EXCLUDES reserves created from asset revaluation, depreciation write-backs, and amalgamation.
Sweat Equity Shares [Sec 2(88)] are equity shares issued to directors or employees at a discount or non-cash for know-how or IPR.

flow.title: Net Worth Calculation Sequence
steps: Add Securities Premium and P&L credit
Deduct accumulated losses and deferred expenses

topics.example: A company revalues its plant and machinery and credits the gain to retained earnings. This revaluation amount must be excluded when computing Net Worth.
remember: Net Worth EXCLUDES revaluation reserves and depreciation write-backs
Free Reserves EXCLUDE unrealised gains and revaluation amounts
Sweat Equity is issued for know-how, value additions, or IPR
mistakes: Including asset revaluation reserves in Net Worth calculations because they were credited to retained earnings.

quiz.q: Which of the following items is EXCLUDED while calculating 'Net Worth' under Section 2(57)?
o: Reserves created out of revaluation of assets
Credit balance of Profit and Loss account
quiz.why: Section 2(57) explicitly excludes reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation, and amalgamation.

quiz.q: Shares issued by a company to its directors or employees for providing intellectual property rights or know-how are called:
quiz.why: Sweat equity shares are defined under Section 2(88) as shares issued for know-how, intellectual property rights, or value additions.

topics.title: Governance, Officers & Related Party Definitions
explain: Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) [Sec 2(51)] includes CEO/MD/Manager, Company Secretary (CS), Whole-Time Director (WTD), and CFO.
Managing Director [Sec 2(54)] is a director entrusted with substantial management powers; must be a director first.
Routine administrative acts (signing cheques, affixing common seal, signing share certificates) are NOT substantial powers.
Officer in Default [Sec 2(60)] includes WTD, KMP, specified directors, persons charged by Board, or all directors if none specified.
Promoter [Sec 2(69)] is named in prospectus/annual return, controls company affairs, or advises the Board (excluding professionals).
Related Party [Sec 2(76)] includes directors, KMPs, relatives, partner firms, private companies with common directors/members, etc.
Relative [Sec 2(77) & Rule 4] includes HUF members, spouse, father, mother, son, son's wife, daughter, daughter's husband, brother, sister (including step-relatives).

flow.title: Identifying Officer in Default
steps: Check for Whole-Time Director or KMP
Check for directors specified by Board
If no director specified, ALL directors liable

topics.example: If a company defaults on share allotment and has no MD, WTD, CS, or specified director, ALL directors of the company are treated as Officers in Default.
remember: A Managing Director must first be an appointed Director
Routine admin tasks (cheques, sealing) != Substantial management powers
Step-father, step-mother, step-son, step-brother, step-sister ARE relatives
mistakes: Treating professional advisers (like an advocate or CA giving advice in professional capacity) as promoters or related parties.

quiz.q: Which of the following routine administrative acts is considered a 'substantial power of management' under Section 2(54)?
o: Affixing common seal to a document
None of these routine administrative acts
quiz.why: Explanation to Section 2(54) clarifies that routine acts like affixing seal, signing cheques, or signing certificates are NOT substantial management powers.

quiz.q: Under Rule 4 of the Companies Rules, 2014, which of the following is NOT included in the list of 'relatives' under Section 2(77)?
quiz.why: Grandfather is not included in the relative list under Rule 4, whereas step-mother, son's wife, and daughter's husband are listed.

topics.title: Financial Reporting, Audit & Corporate Operations
explain: Financial Statement [Sec 2(40)] includes Balance Sheet, P&L Account, Cash Flow Statement, Statement of Changes in Equity, and Explanatory Notes.
Cash Flow Statement Exemption: OPC, Small Company, Dormant Company, and Private Startup Company do NOT need a Cash Flow Statement.
Financial Year [Sec 2(41)] ends on 31st March every year; if incorporated on/after 1st January, FY ends on 31st March of the FOLLOWING year.
Books of Account [Sec 2(13)] include records of cash receipts/payments, sales/purchases, assets/liabilities, and cost items (under Sec 148).
Book and Paper [Sec 2(12)] includes books of account, deeds, vouchers, writings, minutes, and registers in physical or electronic form.
Accounting Standards [Sec 133] and Auditing Standards [Sec 143(10)] are prescribed by Central Government in consultation with NFRA/ICAI.

flow.title: First Financial Year End Determination
steps: If incorporated before 1st January: FY ends 31st March same year
If incorporated on/after 1st January: FY ends 31st March next year
Maximum duration can extend up to 15 months

topics.example: Green Ltd. is incorporated on 3rd January 2026. Its first financial year ends on 31st March 2027 (not 31st March 2026).
remember: Company formed on or after Jan 1 closes its first FY on March 31 of the next year
Cash Flow Statement is exempt for OPC, Small Co, Dormant Co, and Startup Private Co
mistakes: Assuming a company incorporated on January 3rd must close its first financial year on March 31st of the same calendar year.

quiz.q: A company is incorporated on 15th January 2026. What will be its first Financial Year end date under Section 2(41)?
quiz.why: For companies incorporated on or after 1st January of a year, the first financial year ends on 31st March of the following year.

quiz.q: Which of the following entities is NOT exempt from including a Cash Flow Statement in its Financial Statements?
quiz.why: Standard listed public companies must prepare cash flow statements; OPCs, small companies, dormant companies, and startup private companies are exempt.
